description: Everything that measures, labels and organises a drawing: the dimension commands and the styles that drive them, text styles, fields and annotative scaling, and the layer and property commands that decide what is visible, what is editable and what plots. The hyphen-prefixed forms (-LAYER, -DIMSTYLE, -STYLE, -OBJECTSCALE) are what scripts and macros use, because they run entirely at the command line without opening a dialog.

tools.name: DIM
tools.description: The all-in-one dimensioning command introduced in AutoCAD 2016. Hovering over an object previews the dimension type that suits it - a line gives a linear or aligned dimension, a circle gives a diameter, an arc gives a radius or arc length - and clicking places it, after which the command stays active for the next one. Options inside the command switch to baseline, continued, angular and ordinate mode without leaving it.
tools.usage:
DIM
Select objects or specify first extension line origin or [Angular/Baseline/Continue/Ordinate/aliGn/Distribute/Layer/Undo]:
(hover to preview, click to place, Esc or Enter to exit)

parameters.name: Angular (A) / Ordinate (O)
parameters.description: Switch to angular or ordinate dimensioning for the next dimension.

parameters.name: Baseline (B) / Continue (C)
parameters.description: Continue a chain of dimensions from a common baseline or end to end, as DIMBASELINE and DIMCONTINUE do.

parameters.name: aliGn (G) / Distribute (D)
parameters.description: Line up several existing dimensions on one dimension line, or space them evenly - the same job as DIMSPACE.

parameters.name: Layer (L)
parameters.description: Set the layer new dimensions are created on for the rest of the command.

parameters.name: DIMLAYER
parameters.description: System variable holding a default layer for every new dimension, so dimensions never land on whatever layer happens to be current. Set it to a dot to use the current layer.

parameters.name: Undo (U)
parameters.description: Remove the last dimension placed without leaving the command.

tools.example:
; Put every new dimension on its own layer, then dimension a part
-LAYER
M
DIMENSIONS
C
2
DIMENSIONS


DIMLAYER
DIMENSIONS

DIM
(hover over the bottom edge and click to place a linear dimension)
(hover over the bore and click to place a diameter)
B
(pick the next extension line origins for a baseline chain)
tools.notes: DIM is interactive by design: it decides the dimension type from what the cursor is over, which makes it awkward to drive from a script. Use the individual DIMLINEAR, DIMRADIUS and similar commands in scripts and macros where the type must be explicit. The older DIM and DIM1 dimensioning modes from early AutoCAD releases are gone; this command reuses the name.

tools.name: DIMLINEAR
tools.description: Create a horizontal, vertical or rotated linear dimension between two extension line origins, or across a selected object. Press Enter at the first prompt to select a line, polyline segment, arc or circle instead of picking two points, which is faster and keeps the dimension associative to that object. The direction is inferred from where the dimension line is dragged unless Horizontal, Vertical or Rotated is chosen explicitly.
tools.usage:
DIMLINEAR  (alias DLI; also DIMLIN)
Specify first extension line origin or <select object>: <point> | Enter
Specify second extension line origin: <point>
Specify dimension line location or [Mtext/Text/Angle/Horizontal/Vertical/Rotated]: <point> | M | T | A | H | V | R

parameters.name: Text (T)
parameters.description: Replace the measured value with a string. Use <> inside the string to keep the measurement and add a prefix or suffix, for example 2X <>.

parameters.name: Mtext (M)
parameters.description: Open the multiline editor for the dimension text, allowing stacked tolerances and formatting.

parameters.name: Angle (A)
parameters.description: Rotate the dimension text within the dimension line.

parameters.name: Horizontal (H) / Vertical (V)
parameters.description: Force the measurement to the X or Y component of the distance instead of letting the drag direction decide.

parameters.name: Rotated (R)
parameters.description: Measure along a specified angle, which is how auxiliary views and skewed features are dimensioned.

parameters.name: DIMASSOC
parameters.description: System variable controlling associativity: 2 creates associative dimensions that follow the geometry, 1 non-associative, 0 exploded.

tools.example:
; Two points
DIMLINEAR
0,0
100,0
0,-15

; Select an object instead, with a prefix on the value
DIMLINEAR

(select the line)
T
2X <>
0,-30

; AutoLISP
(command "_DIMLINEAR" '(0 0) '(100 0) '(0 -15))
tools.notes: A dimension created while DIMASSOC is 2 updates automatically when the geometry it points at is stretched or scaled; check DIMASSOC before batch-dimensioning, because drawings imported from other systems often arrive with it at 0. DIMLINEAR respects object snaps, so pick with END or INT rather than freehand or the dimension will not stay associative.

tools.name: DIMALIGNED
tools.description: Create a linear dimension whose dimension line is parallel to the two extension line origins, so it measures the true distance rather than a horizontal or vertical component. It is the right command for sloped edges, pitched roofs, bracing and any feature dimensioned along its own axis. As with DIMLINEAR, pressing Enter lets you select an object instead of picking two points.
tools.usage:
DIMALIGNED  (alias DAL; also DIMALI)
Specify first extension line origin or <select object>: <point> | Enter
Specify second extension line origin: <point>
Specify dimension line location or [Mtext/Text/Angle]: <point> | M | T | A

parameters.name: select object
parameters.description: Press Enter to select a line, polyline segment or arc and dimension its full length in one pick.

parameters.name: Text (T)
parameters.description: Override the measured value; <> stands for the measurement itself.

parameters.name: Mtext (M)
parameters.description: Edit the dimension text in the multiline editor.

parameters.name: Angle (A)
parameters.description: Rotation of the dimension text relative to the dimension line.

parameters.name: DIMDEC / DIMLUNIT
parameters.description: Decimal places and linear unit format used for the measured value, set in the current dimension style.

tools.example:
; True length of a sloping brace
DIMALIGNED
0,0
1200,900
-150,150

; Select the object instead
DIMALIGNED

(select the sloping line)
(drag the dimension line clear of the geometry and click)
tools.notes: DIMLINEAR with the Rotated option can produce the same measurement when the dimension line must sit at a different angle from the feature. If an aligned dimension reads a rounded value, raise DIMDEC or check that DIMRND is zero.

tools.name: DIMANGULAR
tools.description: Dimension an angle, defined either by two lines, by an arc, by a circle and two points on it, or by a vertex and two points typed at the prompt. The dimension arc is drawn where you drag it, and dragging to a different side gives the supplementary or reflex angle, which is the usual way to get the angle you actually wanted. The Quadrant option locks the dimension to one quadrant so the text stays put when the dimension is later stretched.
tools.usage:
DIMANGULAR  (alias DAN; also DIMANG)
Select arc, circle, line, or <specify vertex>: <object> | Enter
(vertex form) Specify angle vertex: / Specify first angle endpoint: / Specify second angle endpoint:
Specify dimension arc line location or [Mtext/Text/Angle/Quadrant]: <point> | M | T | A | Q

parameters.name: Select two lines
parameters.description: The most common form: pick one line, then the second, then drag the dimension arc into the quadrant you want.

parameters.name: Select an arc
parameters.description: Dimensions the included angle of the arc directly, using the arc centre as the vertex.

parameters.name: specify vertex
parameters.description: Press Enter to define the angle by a vertex point and two endpoints, for angles with no drawn lines.

parameters.name: Quadrant (Q)
parameters.description: Lock the dimension to a chosen quadrant so the dimension text stays outside the extension lines when the dimension is stretched.

parameters.name: DIMAUNIT / DIMADEC
parameters.description: Angular unit format (decimal degrees, degrees-minutes-seconds, grads, radians) and the number of angular decimal places.

tools.example:
; Angle between two lines
DIMANGULAR
(select first line)
(select second line)
150,120

; Angle from a vertex and two points, shown in deg-min-sec
DIMAUNIT
1
DIMANGULAR

0,0
100,0
70,70
60,30
tools.notes: For angles greater than 180 degrees use the vertex form or drag the arc to the far side; selecting two lines can only ever measure the angle between their infinite extensions. DIMAUNIT 1 gives degrees-minutes-seconds, which surveying and civil drawings normally require.

tools.name: DIMRADIUS
tools.description: Dimension the radius of an arc or circle with a leader that carries the R prefix defined by the dimension style. The dimension line can be dragged inside or outside the curve, and the text placement follows the Fit rules of the current dimension style. A centre mark or centre lines are added automatically according to DIMCEN.
tools.usage:
DIMRADIUS  (alias DRA; also DIMRAD)
Select arc or circle: <object>
Dimension text = <measured value>
Specify dimension line location or [Mtext/Text/Angle]: <point> | M | T | A

parameters.name: Text (T)
parameters.description: Override the value; use <> to keep the measurement, for example R<> TYP.

parameters.name: Angle (A)
parameters.description: Rotate the dimension text.

parameters.name: DIMCEN
parameters.description: Centre mark behaviour: a positive value draws a centre mark of that size, a negative value draws centre lines, 0 draws neither.

parameters.name: DIMTOFL
parameters.description: Forces a dimension line between the extension lines even when the text is placed outside.

parameters.name: DIMRND
parameters.description: Rounds the measured value to the nearest multiple of this number, useful for radii read off scanned drawings.

tools.example:
DIMCEN
2.5
DIMRADIUS
(select the fillet arc)
T
R<> TYP
(place the leader)

; AutoLISP
(command "_DIMRADIUS" (list 50.0 50.0) '(80 80))
tools.notes: Use DIMJOGGED instead when the true centre falls off the sheet. For a full circle most standards call for a diameter rather than a radius, so use DIMDIAMETER on holes and DIMRADIUS on fillets and arcs.

tools.name: DIMDIAMETER
tools.description: Dimension the diameter of a circle or arc, with the diameter symbol supplied by the dimension style prefix. It is the standard way to call out holes and bores, and the text can be forced inside or outside the circle through the Fit settings of the dimension style. The measured value can be overridden to add callouts such as a hole count or a thread note.
tools.usage:
DIMDIAMETER  (alias DDI; also DIMDIA)
Select arc or circle: <object>
Dimension text = <measured value>
Specify dimension line location or [Mtext/Text/Angle]: <point> | M | T | A

parameters.name: Text (T)
parameters.description: Override or extend the value; %%c produces the diameter symbol in a typed override.

parameters.name: Mtext (M)
parameters.description: Open the multiline editor to add a second line such as a depth or thread callout.

parameters.name: DIMCEN
parameters.description: Controls the centre mark or centre lines drawn with the dimension.

parameters.name: DIMTIX / DIMTOFL
parameters.description: Force the text inside the circle, and force a dimension line to be drawn even when the text sits outside.

parameters.name: DIMFIT / Fit options
parameters.description: Dimension style rules deciding what moves outside first when text and arrows do not fit inside the circle.

tools.example:
; Four holes called out from one dimension
DIMDIAMETER
(select one hole)
T
4X <>
(place the leader outside the part)

; Hole with a depth note
DIMDIAMETER
(select the bore)
M
(type: %%c12 THRU)
(place the leader)
tools.notes: In the Text override, <> is replaced by the live measurement and stays associative; typing the number by hand freezes it and it will not update when the geometry changes. DIMCEN should normally match the value used in DIMRADIUS so centre marks look consistent.

tools.name: DIMARC
tools.description: Dimension the length of an arc or of an arc segment inside a polyline, placing the arc length symbol defined by DIMARCSYM. It measures along the curve rather than across the chord, which is what fabrication of curved rails, ducting and sheet metal developments needs. The Partial option dimensions only part of the arc, and Leader adds a leader from the text to the arc when the arc is small.
tools.usage:
DIMARC  (alias DAR)
Select arc or polyline arc segment: <object>
Specify arc length dimension location, or [Mtext/Text/Angle/Partial/Leader]: <point> | M | T | A | P | L

parameters.name: Partial (P)
parameters.description: Specify a start and end point on the arc and dimension only that portion of its length.

parameters.name: Leader (L)
parameters.description: Add a leader from the dimension text to the arc; No Leader removes it again.

parameters.name: Text (T) / Mtext (M)
parameters.description: Override or extend the measured arc length.

parameters.name: DIMARCSYM
parameters.description: Placement of the arc length symbol: 0 before the text, 1 above the text, 2 none.

parameters.name: Angle (A)
parameters.description: Rotation of the dimension text.

tools.example:
DIMARCSYM
1
DIMARC
(select the arc)
(place the dimension outside the curve)

; Only part of a long arc
DIMARC
(select the arc)
P
(pick the start point on the arc)
(pick the end point on the arc)
(place the dimension)
tools.notes: DIMARC works on true arcs and on the arc segments of a polyline, but not on splines or elliptical arcs; convert those or use a dimension override. The extension lines are drawn radially for arcs of 90 degrees or less and orthogonally for larger ones.

tools.name: DIMORDINATE
tools.description: Create an ordinate dimension: a leader with a single value giving the X or Y distance of a feature from the datum, which is the origin of the current UCS. Ordinate dimensioning is standard on sheet metal, printed circuit board outlines and jig-bored parts because it avoids cumulative tolerance. Moving the UCS origin to the datum feature is the essential first step, since every ordinate value is measured from there.
tools.usage:
DIMORDINATE  (alias DOR; also DIMORD)
Specify feature location: <point>
Specify leader endpoint or [Xdatum/Ydatum/Mtext/Text/Angle]: <point> | X | Y | M | T | A

parameters.name: Xdatum (X)
parameters.description: Force the dimension to measure along the X axis regardless of the leader direction.

parameters.name: Ydatum (Y)
parameters.description: Force the dimension to measure along the Y axis.

parameters.name: leader endpoint
parameters.description: Drag roughly vertically for an X ordinate and roughly horizontally for a Y ordinate; AutoCAD infers the axis from the drag direction.

parameters.name: UCS origin
parameters.description: The datum. Use UCS Origin (or UCS Move) to place 0,0 on the datum feature before dimensioning.

parameters.name: Text (T) / Mtext (M)
parameters.description: Override the measured ordinate value.

tools.example:
; Set the datum, then dimension three holes in X and Y
UCS
O
(pick the datum corner)

DIMORDINATE
25,40
X
25,-20

DIMORDINATE
25,40
Y
-20,40

; Return to the world coordinate system afterwards
UCS
W
tools.notes: Ordinate values change the moment the UCS changes, so finish a whole datum set before moving the UCS. Turn ORTHO on while placing the leaders: without it the leaders develop jogs, which is correct behaviour but usually unwanted.

tools.name: DIMBASELINE
tools.description: Continue a linear, angular or ordinate dimension from the first extension line of a base dimension, so several dimensions share a common origin and are stacked at a fixed offset. Baseline dimensioning keeps tolerance from accumulating across a run of features. The stacking offset comes from DIMDLI or, in most modern styles, from the Baseline spacing field of the dimension style.
tools.usage:
DIMBASELINE  (alias DBA; also DIMBASE)
Specify second extension line origin or [Select/Undo] <Select>: <point> | S | U
(repeat for each feature; Enter twice to finish)

parameters.name: Select (S)
parameters.description: Choose a different existing dimension to use as the base dimension, rather than continuing from the last one created.

parameters.name: Undo (U)
parameters.description: Remove the last baseline dimension placed without leaving the command.

parameters.name: DIMDLI
parameters.description: Baseline spacing: the distance each successive dimension line is offset from the previous one.

parameters.name: base dimension
parameters.description: If no dimension was just created, DIMBASELINE prompts for one; the extension line you pick nearest becomes the common origin.

tools.example:
DIMDLI
8
; Base dimension first
DIMLINEAR
0,0
25,0
0,-20

; Then every further feature from the same datum
DIMBASELINE
60,0
95,0
140,0
tools.notes: DIMBASELINE reuses the first extension line origin of the base dimension, so draw the base dimension in the direction you want the run to grow. DIMSPACE is the command to use when a set of baseline dimensions was drawn at the wrong offsets and needs re-spacing afterwards.

tools.name: DIMCONTINUE
tools.description: Continue a linear, angular or ordinate dimension from the second extension line of the previous dimension, producing a chain of dimensions on one line. Chained (running) dimensions are the normal way to dimension a row of holes, a wall with openings or a frame with several bays. The chain shares extension lines, so the drawing stays clean without any manual alignment.
tools.usage:
DIMCONTINUE  (alias DCO; also DIMCONT)
Specify second extension line origin or [Select/Undo] <Select>: <point> | S | U
(repeat for each feature; Enter twice to finish)

parameters.name: Select (S)
parameters.description: Pick a different existing dimension to continue from; the extension line nearest the pick becomes the start of the chain.

parameters.name: Undo (U)
parameters.description: Remove the last continued dimension.

parameters.name: second extension line origin
parameters.description: Each point given becomes the end of one dimension and the start of the next.

parameters.name: DIMASSOC
parameters.description: With DIMASSOC 2 the whole chain stays associative, so stretching the geometry updates every dimension in the run.

tools.example:
; Base dimension, then a running chain along a wall
DIMLINEAR
0,0
900,0
0,-300

DIMCONTINUE
2100,0
3000,0
4200,0


; Continue from an older dimension instead
DIMCONTINUE
S
(select the extension line to continue from)
5000,0
tools.notes: Mixing baseline and chained dimensions on the same feature run is a common drafting error; pick one convention per view. QDIM Continuous produces the same chain from a single selection of geometry and is far quicker on a long run.

tools.name: DIMJOGGED
tools.description: Create a jogged radius dimension, where the dimension line is broken by a zig-zag and the apparent centre is placed at a convenient location instead of the real one. It exists for large-radius arcs whose true centre falls outside the sheet or inside another view, which is common on tank shells, road curves and large fillets. The measured value is still the true radius.
tools.usage:
DIMJOGGED  (alias DJO; also JOG)
Select arc or circle: <object>
Specify center location override: <point>
Specify dimension line location or [Mtext/Text/Angle]: <point> | M | T | A
Specify jog location: <point>

parameters.name: center location override
parameters.description: The false centre the dimension appears to come from; pick a point on the sheet near the arc.

parameters.name: jog location
parameters.description: Where the zig-zag sits along the dimension line.

parameters.name: DIMJOGANG
parameters.description: Angle of the jog in the dimension line, 45 degrees by default; settable between 5 and 90.

parameters.name: Text (T) / Mtext (M)
parameters.description: Override the displayed radius value.

tools.example:
DIMJOGANG
45
DIMJOGGED
(select the large arc)
2000,500
1500,900
1750,700

; The jog can be moved later with grips or
DIMEDIT
H
(select the dimension)
tools.notes: Only the centre is faked; the value reported is the real radius, so the dimension remains truthful and associative. A jogged linear dimension, used when a feature is drawn shortened, is added through the Jog Line option on the Dimension menu (DIMJOGLINE), which is a different command.

tools.name: DIMSPACE
tools.description: Adjust the spacing between parallel linear or angular dimensions so they sit at an equal offset from one another, or set the spacing to zero to make them collinear. It is the tidy-up command for a set of baseline or stacked dimensions that were placed by eye. The Auto option derives the spacing from twice the text height of the base dimension's style, which matches most drafting standards.
tools.usage:
DIMSPACE
Select base dimension: <dimension>
Select dimensions to space: <selection>
Select dimensions to space: Enter
Enter value or [Auto] <Auto>: <distance> | A

parameters.name: base dimension
parameters.description: The dimension that stays where it is; all the others are moved relative to it.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: Explicit spacing between successive dimension lines, in drawing units.

parameters.name: Auto (A)
parameters.description: Spacing calculated automatically as twice the text height of the base dimension's dimension style.

parameters.name: value 0
parameters.description: Aligns the selected dimensions onto the same dimension line as the base dimension, which is how a broken run of dimensions is made collinear.

tools.example:
; Even 10 unit spacing on a baseline stack
DIMSPACE
(select the dimension nearest the part)
(select the other dimensions)

10

; Make a row of dimensions collinear
DIMSPACE
(select the base dimension)
(select the strays)

0
tools.notes: The selected dimensions must be parallel linear dimensions or share a vertex if angular; mixing types produces an error. DIMSPACE only moves dimension lines - it does not change their measured values or their associativity.

tools.name: DIMBREAK
tools.description: Break a dimension, extension or leader line where it crosses other objects, so the drawing reads clearly without exploding anything. The break is a display property of the dimension, not a real gap, so it updates when the dimension or the crossing object moves. Auto maintains the breaks automatically; Manual places a single break at two picked points and does not update.
tools.usage:
DIMBREAK
Select a dimension to add/remove break or [Multiple]: <dimension> | M
Select object to break dimension or [Auto/Manual/Remove] <Auto>: <object> | A | M | R

parameters.name: Auto (A)
parameters.description: Break automatically at every crossing object and keep the breaks updated when anything moves.

parameters.name: Manual (M)
parameters.description: Place one break between two picked points; it is static and will not update.

parameters.name: Remove (R)
parameters.description: Remove all breaks from the selected dimensions.

parameters.name: Multiple (M at first prompt)
parameters.description: Select several dimensions and break them all against the same crossing objects in one operation.

parameters.name: Break size
parameters.description: Gap width, set in the dimension style on the Symbols and Arrows tab; it is a paper-space size when the style is annotative.

tools.example:
; Break a group of dimensions where they cross the centre lines
DIMBREAK
M
(select several dimensions)

A

; Remove the breaks again
DIMBREAK
(select the dimension)
R
tools.notes: Automatic breaks are recalculated on regeneration, so a dimension can appear unbroken until REGEN runs. Manual breaks survive edits to the crossing object but do not follow it, which is why Auto is the better default in a drawing that will keep changing.

tools.name: DIMSTYLE
tools.description: Create, modify, restore, compare and override named dimension styles. A dimension style is a bundle of roughly eighty DIMxxx system variables covering lines, symbols and arrows, text, fit, primary and alternate units and tolerances, and every dimension in the drawing takes its appearance from one. Sub-styles let linear, angular, radius, diameter, ordinate and leader dimensions differ within one parent style.
tools.usage:
DIMSTYLE  (alias D or DST; dialog also DDIM; command-line version -DIMSTYLE)
-DIMSTYLE
Current dimension style: <name>  Annotative: No
Enter a dimension style option [ANnotative/Save/Restore/STatus/Variables/Apply/?] <Restore>:

parameters.name: Save (S) / Restore (R)
parameters.description: Save the current DIMxxx settings as a named style, or make a named style current.

parameters.name: Apply (A)
parameters.description: Update selected dimensions to the current style, clearing any overrides they carry.

parameters.name: STatus / Variables (V)
parameters.description: List the current value of every dimension variable, or the variables of a named style, which is the quickest way to audit a style.

parameters.name: ANnotative (AN)
parameters.description: Create an annotative dimension style, whose text and arrow sizes are paper sizes scaled by the current annotation scale instead of by DIMSCALE.

parameters.name: DIMSCALE
parameters.description: Overall scale factor applied to every size in a non-annotative style: text height, arrow size, extension offsets and gaps. Set it to the plot scale reciprocal (for example 50 for a 1:50 drawing). DIMSCALE 0 scales by the paper space viewport scale.

parameters.name: DIMTXT / DIMASZ / DIMGAP / DIMEXE / DIMEXO
parameters.description: Text height, arrow size, text gap, extension line extension and extension line offset - the sizes that DIMSCALE multiplies.

parameters.name: DIMASSOC
parameters.description: 0 creates exploded dimensions, 1 non-associative, 2 associative (the default). It is a drawing setting, not part of the style.

tools.example:
; Build a 1:50 metric style at the command line
DIMTXT
2.5
DIMASZ
2.5
DIMEXE
1.25
DIMEXO
0.625
DIMDEC
0
DIMSCALE
50
-DIMSTYLE
S
ARCH-50

; Make it current later
-DIMSTYLE
R
ARCH-50

; Push a style change out to existing dimensions
-DIMSTYLE
A
ALL
tools.notes: Use an annotative style OR DIMSCALE, never both: an annotative style ignores DIMSCALE and takes its sizing from CANNOSCALE instead, so the sizes entered are paper sizes in millimetres or inches. DIMOVERRIDE applies a one-off variable change to selected dimensions without touching the style, and -DIMSTYLE Apply removes such overrides.

tools.name: DIMEDIT
tools.description: Edit existing dimensions in bulk: return text to its default position, replace the text, rotate the text, or make the extension lines oblique. The Oblique option is what makes dimensions readable on isometric views, where extension lines must lean to 30 or 150 degrees to sit in the drawing plane. All four options accept a normal selection set, so a whole view can be adjusted in one command.
tools.usage:
DIMEDIT  (alias DED; also DIMED)
Enter type of dimension editing [Home/New/Rotate/Oblique] <Home>: H | N | R | O
Select objects: <selection>
(Oblique) Enter obliquing angle (press ENTER for none):

parameters.name: Home (H)
parameters.description: Move dimension text back to its default position as defined by the dimension style.

parameters.name: New (N)
parameters.description: Replace the text of the selected dimensions; <> in the new string keeps the live measurement.

parameters.name: Rotate (R)
parameters.description: Rotate the dimension text to a given angle; 0 restores it to the default orientation.

parameters.name: Oblique (O)
parameters.description: Slant the extension lines to the given angle, which is how isometric dimensions are made to lie in the correct isoplane.

tools.example:
; Isometric dimensioning: oblique the extension lines
DIMEDIT
O
(select the dimensions on the right-hand face)

30

DIMEDIT
O
(select the dimensions on the left-hand face)

-30

; Add TYP to a set of dimensions
DIMEDIT
N
<> TYP
(select the dimensions)
tools.notes: DIMTEDIT is the companion command that moves and justifies dimension text (Left, Right, Centre, Home, Angle) one dimension at a time. Oblique changes only the appearance of the extension lines; the measured value is unchanged, which is exactly what an isometric drawing needs.

tools.name: QDIM
tools.description: Create a whole set of dimensions from one selection of geometry in a single operation: a continuous chain, a staggered set, a baseline stack, ordinates, or radii and diameters for every selected circle and arc. It is the fastest way to dimension a row of holes or a stepped profile, and it can also edit an existing set by adding or removing datum points. The dimension type chosen persists as the default for the next run.
tools.usage:
QDIM
Select geometry to dimension: <selection>
Select geometry to dimension: Enter
Specify dimension line position, or [Continuous/Staggered/Baseline/Ordinate/Radius/Diameter/datumPoint/Edit/seTtings] <Continuous>:

parameters.name: Continuous (C) / Staggered (S) / Baseline (B)
parameters.description: Chained, staggered or baseline dimension sets generated from the selected geometry.

parameters.name: Ordinate (O)
parameters.description: Ordinate dimensions for every selected feature, measured from the datum point.

parameters.name: Radius (R) / Diameter (D)
parameters.description: A radius or diameter dimension for every arc and circle in the selection.

parameters.name: datumPoint (P)
parameters.description: Set the origin used by the Baseline and Ordinate sets.

parameters.name: Edit (E)
parameters.description: Add or remove dimension points from the set before it is created, which is how unwanted intermediate points are dropped.

parameters.name: seTtings (T)
parameters.description: Choose the default object snap (endpoint or intersection) used to find the dimension points.

tools.example:
; Dimension a row of holes as a chain in one go
QDIM
(window the hole circles)

C
0,-25

; Baseline set from a chosen datum
QDIM
(select the profile)

P
0,0
B
0,-50
tools.notes: QDIM works from the geometry, not from existing dimensions, and it uses the current dimension style. Run it on a clean selection: picking construction lines or hatch boundaries produces extra dimension points that then have to be removed with the Edit option.

tools.name: STYLE
tools.description: Create and modify named text styles, which fix the font, height, width factor, obliquing angle and the backwards, upside-down and vertical flags used by TEXT, MTEXT, dimensions, tables and multileaders. Setting a fixed height in the style makes the height prompt disappear from TEXT and MTEXT, which is how offices enforce a consistent text size. A style can be marked annotative, in which case the height entered is the paper height and the plotted size follows the annotation scale.
tools.usage:
STYLE  (alias ST; command-line version -STYLE)
-STYLE
Enter name of text style or [?] <Standard>: <name>
Specify full font name or font filename (TTF or SHX) <txt>: <font>
Specify height of text or [Annotative] <0.0000>: <height> | A
Specify width factor <1.0000>: / Specify obliquing angle <0>:
Display text backwards? / upside-down? / Vertical? [Yes/No]

parameters.name: font
parameters.description: An SHX shape file (txt, romans, isocp, simplex) or a TrueType font name. SHX fonts plot faster and are the traditional choice; TrueType fonts support bold, italic and Unicode.

parameters.name: height
parameters.description: Fixed text height. Leave it 0 so each text object can be given its own height, or set it to enforce one size everywhere.

parameters.name: Annotative (A)
parameters.description: Make the style annotative: the height given is the paper height and the model-space size follows CANNOSCALE.

parameters.name: width factor
parameters.description: Horizontal expansion or condensation; 0.8 is a common condensed setting for tight title blocks.

parameters.name: obliquing angle
parameters.description: Slant of the characters in degrees; 15 gives the classic italic look used on some engineering standards.

parameters.name: TEXTSTYLE / TEXTSIZE
parameters.description: System variables holding the current text style name and the default text height.

tools.example:
; Annotative style at 3.5 mm on paper
-STYLE
NOTES-3.5
isocp.shx
A
3.5
1
1
0
N
N
N

; Fixed-height SHX style for a title block
-STYLE
TITLE
romans.shx
5
0.8
0
N
N
N
tools.notes: Renaming or redefining a style updates every text object that uses it immediately, including dimension text. The STANDARD style cannot be deleted. FONTALT and FONTMAP decide what happens when a drawing arrives referencing a font that is not installed - without them AutoCAD prompts for a substitute and the text reflows.

tools.name: FIELD
tools.description: Insert a field: a piece of text that holds an expression and displays its current result, such as the drawing filename, the date of the last plot, a sheet set property, a block attribute, or the area of a selected object. Fields keep drawings honest because the value updates rather than having to be retyped. They can be placed as standalone text, inside MTEXT, in table cells, in attributes and in multileader content.
tools.usage:
FIELD
(dialog) Field category: Date & Time | Document | Objects | Other | Plot | SheetSet
Field names / Format / Examples
(the field is inserted at the cursor, or as new text at a picked point)

; Force an update
UPDATEFIELD  (select objects, or ALL)

parameters.name: Objects > Object
parameters.description: Report a property of a selected object, such as the area or perimeter of a polyline, with a chosen format and precision.

parameters.name: Document
parameters.description: Drawing properties from DWGPROPS: title, author, filename, filesize, keywords and custom properties.

parameters.name: Date & Time / Plot
parameters.description: CreateDate, SaveDate, PlotDate, PlotScale, DeviceName and similar values used in title blocks and issue stamps.

parameters.name: Other > DieselExpression
parameters.description: Evaluate a DIESEL expression, which is how conditional and computed field text is produced.

parameters.name: FIELDDISPLAY
parameters.description: 1 (default) shows fields with a grey background on screen so they are recognisable; the background never plots. 0 turns it off.

parameters.name: FIELDEVAL
parameters.description: Bit-coded control of when fields update: 1 on open, 2 on save, 4 on plot, 8 on eTransmit, 16 on regeneration. The default 31 is all of them; 0 stops automatic updating.

tools.example:
FIELDDISPLAY
1
FIELDEVAL
31

; Filename field in a title block
FIELD
(Document > Filename, format: filename only with extension)
(place at the title block text position)

; Area of a room boundary, updating when the boundary is stretched
FIELD
(Objects > Object, select the room polyline, property Area)

; Refresh everything
UPDATEFIELD
ALL
tools.notes: A field placed inside a block attribute is the standard way to build a self-filling title block. Fields evaluate on open, save, plot and regen according to FIELDEVAL, so a value that looks stale usually just needs UPDATEFIELD or a REGEN. Exploding text containing a field converts it to plain text and freezes the value.

tools.name: OBJECTSCALE
tools.description: Add or remove annotation scales from annotative objects, which is what decides at which viewport scales a piece of text, a dimension, a hatch or a block is displayed and at what size. An annotative object stores one representation per supported scale, so the same note can appear correctly sized in a 1:50 and a 1:200 viewport. The command-line form -OBJECTSCALE is the one to use in scripts and macros.
tools.usage:
OBJECTSCALE  (command-line version -OBJECTSCALE)
Select annotative objects: <selection>
(dialog) Annotation Object Scale: Add... / Delete

-OBJECTSCALE
Select annotative objects: <selection>
Enter an option [Add/Delete/?] <Add>: A | D | ?
Enter name of scale to add: <scale name>

parameters.name: Add / Delete
parameters.description: Add a named annotation scale to the selected objects so they display at that scale, or remove one.

parameters.name: CANNOSCALE
parameters.description: The current annotation scale name (for example "1:50"). New annotative objects are created supporting this scale, and CANNOSCALEVALUE holds its numeric value.

parameters.name: ANNOAUTOSCALE
parameters.description: When positive, the current annotation scale is added automatically to annotative objects as the annotation scale is changed, so objects follow new viewport scales without being touched.

parameters.name: ANNOALLVISIBLE
parameters.description: 1 displays annotative objects even when they do not support the current annotation scale; 0 hides them, which is the honest setting when checking a sheet.

parameters.name: SELECTIONANNODISPLAY
parameters.description: Shows all scale representations of an annotative object, faded, while it is selected.

parameters.name: ANNOTATIVEDWG
parameters.description: Marks the whole drawing as annotative so that it scales when inserted as a block into another drawing.

tools.example:
; Give existing notes a second scale so they appear in the 1:200 viewport
CANNOSCALE
1:200
-OBJECTSCALE
(select the annotative text and dimensions)

A
1:200

; Remove a scale that is no longer used
-OBJECTSCALE
(select the objects)

D
1:100

; Check what is annotative and what is not
ANNOALLVISIBLE
0
tools.notes: Annotative scaling replaces the old practice of multiplying sizes by DIMSCALE, LTSCALE and a text-height factor: with an annotative style you enter the paper height once and CANNOSCALE does the arithmetic, and DIMSCALE is ignored for annotative dimension styles. ANNOUPDATE updates an annotative object to match its current style definition, ANNORESET resets the position of an object's scale representations back to that of the current scale, and SCALELISTEDIT adds, removes or resets the list of named scales available in the drawing.

tools.name: LAYER
tools.description: Open the Layer Properties Manager, where layers are created, renamed, deleted and given their on/off, freeze, lock, plot, colour, linetype, lineweight, transparency, plot style and description settings. It also holds per-viewport overrides for colour, linetype, lineweight and transparency, the New VP Freeze column, and the layer filters and groups that keep a large layer list manageable. Layers are the primary organising mechanism of a drawing: what is visible, what plots, and what an object looks like all default to its layer.
tools.usage:
LAYER  (alias LA; palette closed with LAYERCLOSE; command-line version -LAYER)
(palette) Status / Name / On / Freeze / Lock / Plot / Color / Linetype / Lineweight / Transparency / Plot Style / New VP Freeze / VP Freeze / Description
Filters: property filters, group filters, Xref, Unreconciled New Layers

parameters.name: On / Off
parameters.description: Off hides the layer but it is still regenerated and still considered by ZOOM Extents; objects on it are not plotted.

parameters.name: Freeze / Thaw
parameters.description: Frozen layers are not displayed, not regenerated and not plotted, which is faster than Off on large drawings. The current layer cannot be frozen.

parameters.name: Lock / Unlock
parameters.description: Objects on a locked layer are visible and can be snapped to but not selected or edited; they are faded by LAYLOCKFADECTL.

parameters.name: Plot / No plot
parameters.description: A layer can be visible on screen but excluded from plots, which is how construction and reference layers are handled.

parameters.name: VP Freeze / New VP Freeze
parameters.description: Freeze a layer in the current layout viewport only, or set it to be frozen in any newly created viewport.

parameters.name: CLAYER
parameters.description: System variable holding the current layer name; setting it makes that layer current from a script or LISP routine.

parameters.name: LAYEREVAL / LAYERNOTIFY
parameters.description: Control the unreconciled new layer notification, which flags layers that have appeared since the drawing was last checked against its standard.

tools.example:
; Interactive
LAYER
(create DIMENSIONS, colour 2, linetype Continuous, lineweight 0.18)
LAYERCLOSE

; From AutoLISP
(setvar "CLAYER" "DIMENSIONS")
(princ (getvar "CLAYER"))

; Fade locked layers by 70 percent
LAYLOCKFADECTL
70
tools.notes: Layer 0 and layer Defpoints are special: block geometry drawn on layer 0 inherits the properties of the layer the block is inserted on, and Defpoints (created automatically by the first dimension) never plots. Use -LAYER in scripts; the palette cannot be driven by a script. LAYERDLGMODE 0 makes LAYER open the older modal dialog instead of the palette.

tools.name: -LAYER
tools.description: The command-line version of LAYER, and the form every script, macro and AutoLISP routine uses because it never opens a palette. One invocation can chain as many options as needed, each acting on a comma-separated list of layer names with wildcards allowed, before a final Enter exits. Make is the workhorse: it creates the layer if it does not exist and makes it current in one step.
tools.usage:
-LAYER
Enter an option [?/Make/Set/New/ON/OFF/Color/Ltype/LWeight/TRansparency/MATerial/Plot/Freeze/Thaw/LOck/Unlock/stAte/Description]:
(each option prompts for its value and then for a layer name list; Enter with no option exits)

parameters.name: Make (M)
parameters.description: Create the layer if necessary and make it current. The single most useful option in a script.

parameters.name: Set (S) / New (N)
parameters.description: Set makes an existing layer current; New creates one or more layers without making any of them current.

parameters.name: ON / OFF / Freeze (F) / Thaw (T)
parameters.description: Visibility control for a named list of layers. Wildcards work, so OFF with *-REF turns off every reference layer at once.

parameters.name: LOck (LO) / Unlock (U)
parameters.description: Lock or unlock the named layers.

parameters.name: Color (C) / Ltype (L) / LWeight (LW) / TRansparency (TR)
parameters.description: Assign an ACI number or true colour, a loaded linetype, a lineweight in hundredths of a millimetre, and a transparency percentage to the named layers.

parameters.name: Plot (P)
parameters.description: Set whether the named layers plot: answer Y or N, then give the layer list.

parameters.name: stAte (A)
parameters.description: Save and restore named layer states from the command line - the scriptable equivalent of the LAYERSTATE dialog.

parameters.name: Description (D)
parameters.description: Attach a description to the named layers, shown in the Layer Properties Manager.

tools.example:
; Build a small layer standard in one command
-LAYER
M
WALLS
C
3
WALLS
LW
0.35
WALLS
N
DIMENSIONS,TEXT,HATCH
C
2
DIMENSIONS,TEXT
C
8
HATCH
D
Hatching and poche
HATCH


; Turn off every xref reference layer, then make a non-plotting layer
-LAYER
OFF
*-REF
M
CONSTRUCTION
P
N
CONSTRUCTION
tools.notes: Layer names may contain spaces but not the characters < > / \ " : ; ? * | , = or backquote. Wildcards (* ? # @ ~) work in the layer name lists, and ~ negates, so OFF with ~WALLS turns off everything except WALLS. AutoCAD refuses to freeze or turn off the current layer, so make another layer current first - a common cause of a script stalling at an unexpected prompt.

tools.name: LAYERP
tools.description: Undo the last change made to layer settings - on/off, freeze/thaw, lock/unlock, colour, linetype and the other layer properties - without undoing the drawing edits made since. It is the escape hatch after an over-enthusiastic LAYISO or LAYFRZ, and it can be run repeatedly to step back through the layer change history. Tracking is on by default and is controlled by LAYERPMODE.
tools.usage:
LAYERP
Restored previous layer status.

; Turn the tracking on or off
LAYERPMODE  [ON/OFF]

parameters.name: LAYERPMODE
parameters.description: ON (default) records layer setting changes so LAYERP can reverse them; OFF stops tracking and discards the history.

parameters.name: repeat
parameters.description: Run LAYERP again to step further back through the recorded layer changes.

parameters.name: scope
parameters.description: Only layer property changes are reversed. Geometry edits, and the current layer setting, are left alone.

tools.example:
LAYISO
(select an object)

; work on the isolated layer ...

; Put everything back
LAYERP

; Or, specifically for LAYISO
LAYUNISO
tools.notes: LAYERP cannot restore layers that were renamed, purged or deleted, and it cannot undo LAYDEL or LAYMRG - those two are permanent as far as layer history is concerned and need a full UNDO. It also does not track changes made by other applications or by layer states restored through a script.

tools.name: LAYERSTATE
tools.description: Save the complete on/off, freeze, lock, plot, colour, linetype, lineweight, transparency and plot style settings of every layer under a name, and restore them later in one step. Layer states are how a single drawing serves several outputs - a dimensioned sheet, a furniture plan, a services overlay - without duplicating geometry. States can be exported to a .las file and imported into other drawings, and a state can be told to restore only some properties.
tools.usage:
LAYERSTATE  (alias LAS)
(dialog) Layer states list / New / Save / Edit / Rename / Delete / Import / Export
Restore options: which layer properties to restore, turn off layers not found in the state

; Scriptable equivalent
-LAYER
A  (stAte)

parameters.name: New / Save
parameters.description: Record the current layer settings under a name, with an optional description.

parameters.name: Restore
parameters.description: Apply a saved state. Only the properties ticked in the restore options are applied, so a state can change visibility without touching colours.

parameters.name: Export / Import
parameters.description: Write a state to a .las file or read one in, which is how a layer standard is shared between drawings and projects.

parameters.name: Turn off layers not found in layer state
parameters.description: Hides any layer that did not exist when the state was saved, so new layers do not leak into an old view.

parameters.name: Don't list layer states in Xrefs
parameters.description: Filter out the layer states that arrive with attached external references.

parameters.name: viewport overrides
parameters.description: A layer state restored while a layout viewport is active can be applied as viewport property overrides rather than to the whole drawing.

tools.example:
; Save the current arrangement
LAYERSTATE
(New: PLAN-DIMENSIONED, save, close)

; Restore it from a script through -LAYER
-LAYER
A
(choose Restore, then the state name)


; Export for reuse in the next drawing
LAYERSTATE
(select the state, Export to C:/standards/layers/office.las)
tools.notes: A layer state stores settings, not layers: restoring a state into a drawing that lacks some of the layers simply skips them unless the not-found option is used. Layer states are also exposed in the Layer Properties Manager drop-down and on the ribbon, and LAYERSTATE can be driven from LISP through the ACAD_LAYERSTATES dictionary.

tools.name: LAYISO
tools.description: Isolate the layers of the objects you select by hiding or locking every other layer, so you can work on one system without the rest of the drawing in the way. The Settings option decides what happens to the layers that are not isolated: they can be turned off (or VP-frozen in a layout viewport) or locked and faded, the latter keeping them visible for reference and snapping. LAYUNISO reverses the operation.
tools.usage:
LAYISO
Current setting: Hide layers, Viewports=Vpfreeze
Select objects on the layer(s) to be isolated or [Settings]: <selection> | S
(Settings) Enter setting for layers not isolated [Off/Lock and fade] <Off>:
(Off, in a layout) Enter a setting for layers not isolated [Vpfreeze/Off] <Vpfreeze>:

parameters.name: Settings > Off
parameters.description: Turn the other layers off entirely so nothing else is displayed or selectable.

parameters.name: Settings > Lock and fade
parameters.description: Lock and fade the other layers instead of hiding them, keeping them visible as a reference you can still snap to.

parameters.name: Settings > Vpfreeze
parameters.description: In a layout viewport, freeze the other layers in that viewport only, leaving the rest of the sheet intact.

parameters.name: LAYLOCKFADECTL
parameters.description: Fade percentage applied to locked layers, from -90 to 90. A negative value stores the setting but disables the fading.

parameters.name: selection
parameters.description: Every layer represented in the selection set is isolated, so several layers can be isolated at once.

tools.example:
LAYLOCKFADECTL
70
LAYISO
S
L

(select one object on the ELECTRICAL layer and one on the LIGHTING layer)

; ... edit the isolated layers ...

LAYUNISO
tools.notes: Use LAYUNISO rather than LAYERP to reverse LAYISO: LAYUNISO restores exactly the state before the isolation, including the lock and fade settings. Objects on a locked, faded layer can still be used for object snaps, which is usually why Lock and fade is preferred over Off.

tools.name: LAYUNISO
tools.description: Restore all the layers that were hidden or locked by the most recent LAYISO command, returning the drawing to the state it had before the isolation. It is the designated companion to LAYISO and is more reliable than LAYERP for that job, because it knows exactly which layers LAYISO touched. Layer changes made deliberately after the LAYISO are preserved.
tools.usage:
LAYUNISO
Layers isolated by LAYISO command have been restored.

parameters.name: scope
parameters.description: Only the layers hidden or locked by the last LAYISO are affected; layers turned off by other means stay off.

parameters.name: later changes
parameters.description: Layer settings altered after LAYISO ran are not reverted, so intentional changes during the isolation survive.

parameters.name: no prior LAYISO
parameters.description: If LAYISO was not used since the drawing was opened, the command reports that there is nothing to restore.

tools.example:
LAYISO
(select an object on the layer to work on)

; ... draw and edit ...

LAYUNISO
tools.notes: LAYUNISO remembers only the last isolation, so running LAYISO twice in succession loses the original state - LAYERP may then be needed to step further back. It does not thaw layers that were frozen manually, nor does it undo a viewport freeze applied outside LAYISO.

tools.name: LAYOFF
tools.description: Turn off the layer of each object selected, by picking the object rather than hunting for the layer name in a list. It is the quickest way to clear clutter in an unfamiliar drawing where the layer naming is not obvious. Settings control whether a selection inside a block affects the block's own layer or the layer of the nested object, and how the command behaves in a layout viewport.
tools.usage:
LAYOFF
Current settings: Viewports=Vpfreeze, Block nesting level=Block
Select an object on the layer to be turned off or [Settings/Undo]: <object> | S | U
(Settings) Enter setting for layer off [Viewports/Block selection] <Block selection>:

parameters.name: Settings > Viewports
parameters.description: In a layout, choose whether the layer is VP-frozen in the current viewport only or turned off throughout the drawing.

parameters.name: Settings > Block selection > Block
parameters.description: Selecting an object inside a block turns off the layer the block reference itself sits on.

parameters.name: Settings > Block selection > Entity
parameters.description: Turns off the layer of the nested object actually picked, leaving the block reference visible.

parameters.name: Settings > Block selection > None
parameters.description: Blocks and xrefs are treated as single objects and nested selection is ignored.

parameters.name: Undo (U)
parameters.description: Turn the last layer back on without leaving the command.

tools.example:
LAYOFF
S
B
E

(pick an object on each layer to hide)
(pick another)


; Bring everything back
LAYON
tools.notes: Turning off the current layer prompts for confirmation, because new objects will then be drawn invisibly. Off is not the same as frozen: an off layer is still regenerated and is still included by ZOOM Extents, so use LAYFRZ on very large drawings where regeneration time matters.

tools.name: LAYON
tools.description: Turn on every layer in the drawing in one command, undoing the effect of any number of LAYOFF operations or manual off settings. It is the quick way to see everything again before checking, plotting or auditing a drawing you have been working in for a while. Frozen layers are unaffected and still need LAYTHW.
tools.usage:
LAYON
All layers have been turned on.

parameters.name: scope
parameters.description: Every layer in the drawing, including xref-dependent layers, is turned on regardless of how it was turned off.

parameters.name: frozen layers
parameters.description: Not affected - a frozen layer stays invisible until LAYTHW or the Thaw option of -LAYER is used.

parameters.name: viewport freeze
parameters.description: Layers frozen in individual layout viewports remain frozen there.

tools.example:
; Reveal everything before a final check
LAYON
LAYTHW
ZOOM
E

; Then restore the working arrangement
LAYERSTATE
(restore the saved state)
tools.notes: Save a layer state before running LAYON and LAYTHW on a drawing with a carefully arranged view, otherwise the arrangement has to be rebuilt by hand. There is no selective version of this command: use -LAYER ON with a wildcard layer list to turn on just part of the drawing.

tools.name: LAYFRZ
tools.description: Freeze the layer of each object selected. A frozen layer is not displayed, not regenerated and not plotted, which makes freezing the faster choice over turning layers off on large drawings and on drawings with many external references. As with LAYOFF, the Settings option decides how nested objects inside blocks and xrefs are interpreted and whether the freeze applies to the whole drawing or only the current viewport.
tools.usage:
LAYFRZ
Current settings: Viewports=Vpfreeze, Block nesting level=Block
Select an object on the layer to be frozen or [Settings/Undo]: <object> | S | U
(Settings) Enter setting type for [Viewports/Block selection] <Block selection>:

parameters.name: Settings > Viewports > Vpfreeze
parameters.description: In a layout, freeze the layer only in the current viewport, leaving other viewports unaffected.

parameters.name: Settings > Viewports > Freeze
parameters.description: Freeze the layer throughout the drawing.

parameters.name: Settings > Block selection
parameters.description: Block, Entity or None - whether picking a nested object freezes the block's layer or the nested object's layer.

parameters.name: Undo (U)
parameters.description: Thaw the last layer frozen without leaving the command.

parameters.name: current layer
parameters.description: The current layer cannot be frozen; AutoCAD reports this and leaves it thawed.

tools.example:
LAYFRZ
S
V
F

(pick an object on each layer to freeze)


; Thaw everything again
LAYTHW
tools.notes: Freezing and thawing forces a regeneration, so on a very large drawing turning layers off can feel quicker even though frozen layers are cheaper afterwards. Xref layers can be frozen individually, which is the normal way to hide part of an attached background without detaching it.

tools.name: LAYTHW
tools.description: Thaw every frozen layer in the drawing in one command, so their objects are displayed, regenerated and plotted again. It is the counterpart to LAYFRZ and the usual first step when taking over a drawing whose visibility state is unknown. Layers that were turned off remain off and need LAYON.
tools.usage:
LAYTHW
All layers have been thawed.

parameters.name: scope
parameters.description: Thaws all layers frozen in the drawing as a whole.

parameters.name: viewport freeze
parameters.description: Layers frozen in individual layout viewports are not thawed by this command; clear those in the Layer Properties Manager VP Freeze column or with the VPLAYER command.

parameters.name: regeneration
parameters.description: Thawing triggers a regeneration, which can take noticeable time on a large drawing with many xrefs.

tools.example:
; Reveal everything in an unfamiliar drawing
LAYTHW
LAYON
LAYULK
ZOOM
E

; Record what you found before changing it
LAYERSTATE
(New: AS-RECEIVED)
tools.notes: Run LAYERSTATE first if the current arrangement matters - LAYTHW is a blunt instrument and LAYERP will not always get a complex arrangement back. VPLAYER gives per-viewport freeze and thaw control from the command line, which LAYTHW deliberately does not touch.

tools.name: LAYLCK
tools.description: Lock the layer of a selected object. Objects on a locked layer stay visible and can be used for object snaps and for measuring, but cannot be selected, edited or deleted, which protects background information, xref-like reference drawings and survey data from accidental change. Locked layers are displayed faded by the amount set in LAYLOCKFADECTL so it is obvious which parts of the drawing are protected.
tools.usage:
LAYLCK
Select an object on the layer to be locked: <object>
Layer "<name>" has been locked.

parameters.name: select object
parameters.description: Pick any object on the layer to be locked; the command locks that object's layer and ends.

parameters.name: LAYLOCKFADECTL
parameters.description: Fade percentage for locked layers, -90 to 90. Positive values fade, negative values keep the setting but display the layer normally.

parameters.name: current layer
parameters.description: The current layer can be locked. New objects are still created on it but cannot then be edited, which surprises people.

parameters.name: object snaps
parameters.description: Snapping to objects on a locked layer still works, which is what makes locking preferable to turning a reference layer off.

tools.example:
LAYLOCKFADECTL
50
LAYLCK
(pick an object on the survey background)

; Unlock it again
LAYULK
(pick an object on the same layer)
tools.notes: Locked layers still plot: locking controls editing, not visibility or output. Use the No plot flag in the Layer Properties Manager or -LAYER Plot to keep a layer visible on screen but out of the plot.

tools.name: LAYULK
tools.description: Unlock the layer of a selected object, reversing LAYLCK. Because objects on a locked layer cannot normally be selected, this command is written to accept a pick on a locked object specifically so the layer can be identified without looking up its name. It affects one layer per run.
tools.usage:
LAYULK
Select an object on the layer to be unlocked: <object>
Layer "<name>" has been unlocked.

parameters.name: select object
parameters.description: Pick an object on the locked layer; the pick works even though the object cannot otherwise be selected.

parameters.name: scope
parameters.description: One layer per run. Use -LAYER Unlock with a wildcard list to unlock many layers at once.

parameters.name: fading
parameters.description: The fade applied by LAYLOCKFADECTL disappears as soon as the layer is unlocked.

tools.example:
LAYULK
(pick an object on the faded, locked layer)

; Unlock everything from a script instead
-LAYER
U
*
tools.notes: -LAYER Unlock with * unlocks every layer in one go, which is the usual first step when taking over someone else's drawing. LAYERP can also reverse a lock, since locking is a tracked layer property change.

tools.name: LAYMCUR
tools.description: Make the layer of a selected object the current layer, without having to find its name in the layer list. It is the fastest way to continue drawing on the same layer as something already in the drawing, and it is the command behind the Make Current button on the Layers ribbon panel. The result is simply a change to the CLAYER system variable.
tools.usage:
LAYMCUR
Select object whose layer will become current: <object>
<name> is now the current layer.

parameters.name: select object
parameters.description: Any object; its layer becomes current. Picking a nested object inside a block uses the block reference's layer.

parameters.name: CLAYER
parameters.description: System variable that holds the current layer name. Setting it directly is the scripted equivalent of this command.

parameters.name: frozen or off layers
parameters.description: An off layer can be made current (with a warning); a frozen layer cannot be current, so it is thawed first.

tools.example:
LAYMCUR
(pick an existing wall line)
LINE
0,0
5000,0


; Equivalent in AutoLISP
(setvar "CLAYER" (cdr (assoc 8 (entget (car (entsel))))))
tools.notes: LAYCUR does the opposite job - it moves selected objects onto the current layer. Both are Express Tools commands that became core AutoCAD, and both appear on the Home ribbon Layers panel.

tools.name: LAYDEL
tools.description: Delete a layer and everything drawn on it, including objects inside block definitions, and then purge the layer from the drawing. It succeeds where PURGE fails, because PURGE will not remove a layer that still contains objects. It is the tool for stripping a contractor's title block layer or a redundant system out of a drawing completely.
tools.usage:
LAYDEL
Select object on layer to delete or [Name]: <object> | N
(Name) (dialog) select one or more layers by name
Select object on layer to delete or [Name/Undo]: Enter
You are about to permanently delete layer "<name>" from this drawing.  Do you wish to continue? [Yes/No] <No>:

parameters.name: Name (N)
parameters.description: Choose the layers from a list by name instead of picking an object, which is safer when the layer is empty on screen.

parameters.name: Undo (U)
parameters.description: Remove the last layer from the delete list before confirming.

parameters.name: confirmation
parameters.description: The command asks for explicit confirmation before deleting, because the operation is far-reaching.

parameters.name: block definitions
parameters.description: Objects on the layer are removed from block definitions as well, so every insertion of the block changes.

parameters.name: protected layers
parameters.description: Layer 0, xref-dependent layers and the current layer cannot be deleted.

tools.example:
LAYDEL
N
(choose OLD-TITLEBLOCK and SURVEY-2019 from the list)

Y

; Tidy up whatever is left
PURGE
A

N
tools.notes: LAYERP cannot bring a deleted layer back - only a full UNDO immediately afterwards will. Because LAYDEL edits block definitions, check that no other system depends on those blocks before running it, and work on a copy of an issued drawing.

tools.name: LAYMRG
tools.description: Merge one or more layers into a target layer: every object on the source layers is moved to the target and the source layers are then purged from the drawing. It is the standard way to collapse a messy layer list, for example consolidating a dozen inherited text layers into a single TEXT layer. Objects inside block definitions are moved as well.
tools.usage:
LAYMRG
Select object on layer to merge or [Name]: <object> | N
Select object on layer to merge or [Name/Undo]: Enter
Select object on target layer or [Name]: <object> | N
****  You are about to merge layer "<a>" into layer "<b>".  Do you wish to continue? [Yes/No] <No>:

parameters.name: Name (N)
parameters.description: Pick the source or target layers from a list instead of selecting objects - the reliable way to include empty or hidden layers.

parameters.name: Undo (U)
parameters.description: Remove the last layer from the merge list before confirming.

parameters.name: target layer
parameters.description: The layer everything is moved onto. It keeps its own colour, linetype and lineweight, so the merged objects take on its appearance where their properties are ByLayer.

parameters.name: source layers
parameters.description: Purged after the merge. They cannot be the current layer, and xref-dependent layers cannot be merged.

tools.example:
LAYMRG
N
(select TEXT-OLD, NOTES1, ANNO-TXT)


N
(select TEXT)

Y

; Confirm the layer list afterwards
-LAYER
?
*
tools.notes: LAYERP will not undo a merge, and neither will LAYERSTATE, because the source layers no longer exist - use UNDO straight away if the merge was wrong. Objects with explicit colours or linetypes keep them after the merge; run SETBYLAYER on the target layer afterwards if the whole set should follow the new layer.

tools.name: LAYTRANS
tools.description: Translate the layers of the current drawing into a different layer standard, mapping each existing layer onto a layer taken from another drawing, template or standards file. It renames layers and applies the standard's colours, linetypes and lineweights in one pass, and the mapping can be saved and reused on the rest of a project. This is the tool for bringing a consultant's drawing onto the office standard without redrawing anything.
tools.usage:
LAYTRANS
(dialog) Translate From: layers in this drawing | Translate To: Load... a DWG, DWT or DWS
Map / Map same / New... / Edit / Remove / Save... the mapping to a .dws
Settings: force object colour, linetype, lineweight and transparency to ByLayer; translate objects in blocks; write transaction log
Translate

parameters.name: Load
parameters.description: Read the target layer standard from a DWG, DWT or DWS file; New creates a target layer that does not exist in that file.

parameters.name: Map same
parameters.description: Automatically map every layer whose name matches one in the standard, leaving only the exceptions to be mapped by hand.

parameters.name: Force object colour/linetype/lineweight to ByLayer
parameters.description: Strips explicit object properties during the translation so the new layer settings actually take effect.

parameters.name: Translate objects in blocks
parameters.description: Applies the translation inside block definitions as well as to top-level objects.

parameters.name: Write transaction log
parameters.description: Records what was translated in a .log file beside the drawing, which is useful evidence on a controlled project.

parameters.name: Save
parameters.description: Store the mapping in a .dws file so the same translation can be applied to every drawing in the package.

tools.example:
LAYTRANS
(Load C:/standards/office-standard.dwt)
(Map same, then map the remaining layers by hand)
(Settings: tick Force object colour to ByLayer and Translate objects in blocks)
(Save mapping to C:/standards/consultant-map.dws)
(Translate)

; Then clean up
PURGE
A

N
tools.notes: Translation renames layers rather than merging them, so two source layers mapped to one target are effectively merged and cannot be separated again afterwards. Run it on a copy first and keep the transaction log; the Force to ByLayer settings are what most people forget, leaving objects visually unchanged despite a correct layer list.

tools.name: LINETYPE
tools.description: Load linetype definitions into the drawing from a .lin file and set the current linetype for new objects. AutoCAD ships acad.lin (imperial) and acadiso.lin (metric), whose definitions differ by a factor of 25.4, and only loaded linetypes can be assigned to a layer or an object. The current linetype is normally left at ByLayer so that linetype is controlled by the layer, which is the whole point of layers.
tools.usage:
LINETYPE  (alias LT; also LTYPE and DDLTYPE; command-line version -LINETYPE)
-LINETYPE
Enter an option [?/Create/Load/Set]: ? | C | L | S
(Load) Enter linetype(s) to load: <names or *>
Enter file name <acadiso.lin>:

parameters.name: Load (L)
parameters.description: Load one or more linetype definitions, by name or with wildcards, from a .lin file into the drawing.

parameters.name: Set (S)
parameters.description: Make a loaded linetype current for new objects. ByLayer is the normal setting.

parameters.name: Create (C)
parameters.description: Define a simple dash-dot linetype at the command line and append it to a .lin file.

parameters.name: CELTYPE
parameters.description: System variable holding the current object linetype: ByLayer, ByBlock or a loaded linetype name.

parameters.name: CELTSCALE
parameters.description: Linetype scale applied to newly created objects individually, multiplied by LTSCALE for the final appearance.

parameters.name: acad.lin / acadiso.lin
parameters.description: The imperial and metric definition files; the metric definitions are 25.4 times larger, which is why a drawing can look like it has continuous lines after loading from the wrong file.

tools.example:
; Load the linetypes a drawing standard needs, in a script
FILEDIA
0
-LINETYPE
L
CENTER,HIDDEN,DASHED,PHANTOM
acadiso.lin


; Assign them to layers and keep objects ByLayer
-LAYER
L
CENTER
CENTRELINES
L
HIDDEN
HIDDEN


CELTYPE
ByLayer
tools.notes: Set FILEDIA 0 before -LINETYPE in scripts or the file selection dialog stops them. A linetype that appears continuous almost always means the scale is wrong rather than the linetype being unloaded: check LTSCALE, CELTSCALE, PSLTSCALE and MSLTSCALE before reloading anything.

tools.name: LTSCALE
tools.description: Set the global linetype scale factor, which multiplies the dash and gap lengths of every non-continuous linetype in the drawing. Getting it right is what makes centre lines and hidden lines read correctly at the plotted scale, and it is the single most common cause of linetypes appearing solid. Changing it forces a regeneration.
tools.usage:
LTSCALE  (alias LTS)
Enter new linetype scale factor <1.0000>: <value>
Regenerating model.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: Global multiplier. A traditional starting point is the plot scale reciprocal, or about half of it, so a 1:50 drawing might use 25 to 50.

parameters.name: CELTSCALE
parameters.description: Per-object linetype scale for newly created objects; the displayed dash length is LTSCALE multiplied by the object's own linetype scale.

parameters.name: PSLTSCALE
parameters.description: 1 (default) makes linetypes display at the same dash length in paper space regardless of each viewport's zoom, which is what mixed-scale sheets need. 0 scales them by the viewport.

parameters.name: MSLTSCALE
parameters.description: 1 (default) scales linetypes in model space by the current annotation scale, so they look right while drawing at an annotative scale.

parameters.name: REGEN
parameters.description: A regeneration is needed for the change to appear; LTSCALE triggers one automatically.

tools.example:
; Metric sheet plotted at 1:50
LTSCALE
25
PSLTSCALE
1
MSLTSCALE
1
REGENALL

; Fix one badly scaled object instead of the whole drawing
CHPROP
(select the object)

LTS
0.5
tools.notes: With PSLTSCALE 1 the linetype scale is interpreted in paper space units, so LTSCALE 1 is often correct for viewports on a properly set up sheet - set it once per office standard rather than guessing per drawing. The Properties palette exposes the per-object Linetype scale, which overrides nothing but multiplies LTSCALE for that object.

tools.name: LWEIGHT
tools.description: Set the current lineweight for new objects and control how lineweights are displayed: the units used, whether display is on in model space, and the display scale slider. Lineweights are a real object property stored in hundredths of a millimetre, and they are an alternative to controlling plotted line thickness through colour-dependent plot styles. Most offices choose one system or the other and stay with it.
tools.usage:
LWEIGHT  (alias LW; also LINEWEIGHT; command-line version -LWEIGHT)
(dialog) Lineweights list / Units for Listing (millimetres or inches) / Display Lineweight / Default / Adjust Display Scale

-LWEIGHT
Enter default lineweight for new objects or [?]: <value> | ByLayer | ByBlock | Default

parameters.name: CELWEIGHT
parameters.description: Current object lineweight: -1 ByLayer, -2 ByBlock, -3 Default, or a value in hundredths of a millimetre such as 30 for 0.30 mm.

parameters.name: LWDEFAULT
parameters.description: The value used by the Default lineweight, in hundredths of a millimetre; 25 (0.25 mm) is the out-of-the-box setting.

parameters.name: LWDISPLAY
parameters.description: Whether lineweights are shown in the current tab. It is stored per tab, so model space and each layout have their own setting.

parameters.name: LWUNITS
parameters.description: 0 displays lineweights in inches, 1 in millimetres.

parameters.name: Adjust Display Scale
parameters.description: Display-only thickness scaling in model space; it does not affect plotted output.

tools.example:
LWUNITS
1
LWDEFAULT
25
LWDISPLAY
ON

; Keep objects ByLayer and set the weight on the layer
CELWEIGHT
-1
-LAYER
LW
0.50
WALLS
LW
0.18
DIMENSIONS,TEXT
tools.notes: Lineweights in model space are drawn at a display width that is not related to their plotted width, so never judge them on screen - plot preview is the only reliable check. If the plot ignores lineweights, check that Plot object lineweights is ticked in the plot dialog and that the plot style table is not overriding them.

tools.name: COLOR
tools.description: Set the colour assigned to new objects, either as ByLayer, ByBlock, an AutoCAD Color Index number from 1 to 255, a true colour, or a colour from a colour book such as Pantone or RAL. The standard drafting practice is to leave it at ByLayer so that colour is controlled entirely by the layer, which in turn drives plotted lineweight when a colour-dependent plot style table is used.
tools.usage:
COLOR  (alias COL; also COLOUR; command-line version -COLOR)
-COLOR
New object color [Truecolor/COlorbook] <ByLayer>: <1-255> | ByLayer | ByBlock | T | CO
(Truecolor) Red,Green,Blue: 255,0,0

parameters.name: ByLayer
parameters.description: New objects take the colour of the layer they are drawn on. The normal setting in any managed drawing.

parameters.name: ByBlock
parameters.description: Objects are drawn white or black until they are made into a block, after which they take the colour of the block reference. Used when defining symbol geometry.
AutoCAD Color Index. 1 red, 2 yellow, 3 green, 4 cyan, 5 blue, 6 magenta, 7 white/black - the seven that colour-dependent plot style tables are usually built around.

parameters.name: Truecolor (T)
parameters.description: 24-bit RGB colour entered as R,G,B. True colours are ignored by colour-dependent plot style tables, which only understand the 255 index colours.

parameters.name: COlorbook (CO)
parameters.description: Choose a named colour from an installed colour book file.

parameters.name: CECOLOR
parameters.description: System variable holding the current object colour setting.

tools.example:
; Keep drawing ByLayer
-COLOR
ByLayer

; Block geometry that should inherit the insertion layer's colour
-COLOR
ByBlock
-LAYER
S
0


; From AutoLISP
(setvar "CECOLOR" "BYLAYER")
tools.notes: Objects drawn with an explicit colour override their layer, which is what makes drawings hard to manage; SETBYLAYER puts them back. If the office uses a colour-dependent plot style table (.ctb), avoid true colours entirely, because only the 255 index colours have a pen assignment in a .ctb.

tools.name: SETBYLAYER
tools.description: Change the colour, linetype, lineweight, transparency and material of selected objects back to ByLayer, undoing hard-coded property overrides. It is the repair command for drawings received from other offices where everything was drawn in an explicit colour, and it is the step that makes a layer standard actually take effect. It can optionally reach inside block references and convert ByBlock properties as well.
tools.usage:
SETBYLAYER
Current active settings: Color Linetype Lineweight Transparency
Select objects or [Settings]: <selection> | S
Change ByBlock to ByLayer? [Yes/No] <Yes>:
Include blocks? [Yes/No] <Yes>:

parameters.name: Settings (S)
parameters.description: Choose which properties are reset - colour, linetype, lineweight, material, transparency - before selecting objects.

parameters.name: Change ByBlock to ByLayer
parameters.description: Also converts properties set to ByBlock, which otherwise stay as they are.

parameters.name: Include blocks
parameters.description: Applies the change to the objects inside block references as well as to top-level objects.

parameters.name: SETBYLAYERMODE
parameters.description: Bit-coded system variable holding the active settings: 1 colour, 2 linetype, 4 lineweight, 8 material, 16 transparency.

parameters.name: selection
parameters.description: ALL is the usual answer when normalising a whole drawing; work on a copy the first time.

tools.example:
; Normalise a drawing received from a consultant
SETBYLAYERMODE
23
SETBYLAYER
ALL

Y
Y

; Then set the real properties on the layers
-LAYER
C
3
WALLS
LW
0.50
WALLS
tools.notes: Run this before LAYTRANS or LAYMRG, otherwise objects keep their explicit colours and the new layer settings appear to do nothing. Including blocks changes the block definitions, so every insertion in the drawing is affected - check any blocks that were deliberately drawn in fixed colours first.
